content: The Primary Health Care Quality Improvement Guide: Module 1 focuses on strategies to prevent unplanned pregnancies through the enhancement of outpatient family planning services. This guide, published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2024, provides a structured approach to assess and improve the quality of primary health care services. It emphasizes the importance of universal access to family planning as a fundamental human right, enabling women to make informed decisions about the number, timing, and spacing of their children. The guide highlights that increasing access to contraception can significantly reduce maternal deaths by approximately 30% and child mortality by up to 20%. It also underscores the broader benefits of family planning, including promoting universal education, empowering women, reducing poverty, and supporting environmental sustainability. Despite these advantages, many women in the WHO Western Pacific Region still face barriers to accessing modern contraceptive methods, leading to high rates of unintended pregnancies. In some areas, over half of all births are unintended, and one in four adolescent girls becomes a mother. The guide identifies common obstacles to contraceptive use, such as health concerns, fear of side effects, and incorrect usage. However, missed opportunities and unaddressed concerns often hinder the delivery of these services. To address these challenges, the guide outlines a bottom-up planning approach that engages local health staff in identifying and solving problems. By collecting and monitoring facility data, progress can be tracked, and continuous improvements can be made. The guide also provides tools, such as checklists, to assess the quality of clinical care, policies, supplies, and environments. These tools help identify areas for improvement and develop actionable plans at the facility, district, provincial, and national levels. The guide emphasizes the importance of systems investments to improve family planning services. Key actions include enhancing the capacity of the health workforce, ensuring equitable distribution of staff trained in long-acting contraceptive methods, and making these methods widely available without financial burden on families. It also calls for addressing the unique needs of vulnerable groups, such as adolescents, minority populations, and women with disabilities, by implementing community-based strategies and building resilient health systems. The guide provides detailed instructions for conducting continuous monitoring and periodic evaluations of family planning services. It recommends pairing facility staff with trained external facilitators to assess services, develop quality improvement plans, and track progress. For periodic evaluations, external teams assess multiple facilities to inform broader systems planning. The guide also includes tools for synthesizing findings, completing monitoring and evaluation tables, and using data to develop annual implementation plans. In summary, this guide serves as a comprehensive resource for improving the quality of primary health care services to prevent unplanned pregnancies.
